## The 4 steps in any data analysis

1. Finding data
2. Cleaning data to combine several data sources
3. **Producing knowledge out from data (summary statistics, regression analysis summarised via tables and graphs)**
4. Interpreting the results (writing)

## Example of a graph made with `R` {#sec-ex-graph-ggplot2}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Monthly number of deaths in France (2020–2025). Source: [Insee](https://www.insee.fr/en/statistiques/serie/000436394) (ref.: 000436394). ([R Codes](#sec-appendix-codes-graph))"
library(tidyverse)

# Source: https://www.insee.fr/en/statistiques/serie/000436394
file <- "../data/deces_france_insee/monthly_values.csv"
deces <- read_csv2(file, skip = 4, col_names = c("period", "deaths", "codes"))

deces <-
  deces |>
  mutate(
    date = ym(period),
    month = month(date, label = TRUE),
    year = year(date)
  )

data_plot_deaths <- deces |>
  mutate(
    year_excess = case_when(
      year == 2003 ~ "2003 (Drought)",
      year == 2020 ~ "2020 (Covid-19)",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    year_excess = factor(
      year_excess,
      levels = c("2003 (Drought)", "2020 (Covid-19)", "Other")
    )
  )

p_deaths <- ggplot(
  data = data_plot_deaths,
  mapping = aes(x = month, y = deaths, group = year, colour = year_excess)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = .8) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    NULL, values = c(
      "2003 (Drought)" = "blue",
      "2020 (Covid-19)" = "red",
      "Other" = "darkgray"
    )
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Deaths") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_number(suffix = "", scale = 1, big.mark = ",")
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p_deaths
```


<!-- ![Monthly number of deaths in France (2020–2025). Source: [Insee](https://www.insee.fr/en/statistiques/serie/000436394) (ref.: 000436394)](figs/seance_3/p_deaths.pdf) -->

# A grammar of graphics {.part}

## Visualization with `{ggplot2}`

- There are multiple packages to produce graphs in `R`.
  - The `{base}` and `{ggplot2}` packages offer plot functions I rely on the most.
- Here, we will introduce only functions from `{ggplot2}`.
- With this package, plots are created following a "[g]{.gras-firstCol}rammar of [g]{.gras-firstCol}raphics" and are constructed by adding <span class="hl-blue">layers</span> to one another.
- The (awesome) official documentation: [https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/)

```r
library(ggplot2)
```

::: {.warning}
<span class="box-title">Disclaimer</span>
The slides are strongly inspired by the [🌐 introduction](https://stats.oarc.ucla.edu/r/seminars/ggplot2_intro/) provided by de @bruin_2024.
:::

## What is a grammar of graphics?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
[![](figs/seance_3/cover-ggplot2.jpg)](https://ggplot2-book.org/)
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
- A grammar of a **language** defines the rules of structuring words and phrases into meaningful expressions.
- Similarly, a grammar of **graphics** defines the rules of structuring mathematical and aesthetic elements into a meaningful graph.
- @wilkinson2005grammar designed the grammar upon which `{ggplot2}` is based.
- To learn with a book: @wickham2016ggplot2.
:::
::::

## The main elements in a `ggplot2` graph

- <span class="hl-blue">Data</span>: variables mapped to aesthetic features of the graph.
- <span class="hl-blue">Geoms</span>: objects/shapes on the graph.
- <span class="hl-blue">Stats</span>: statistical transformations that summarize data (e.g. mean, confidence intervals).
- <span class="hl-blue">Scales</span>: mappings of aesthetic values to data values. Legends and axes visualize scales.
- <span class="hl-blue">Coordinate systems</span>: the plane on which data are mapped on the graphic.
- <span class="hl-blue">Faceting</span>: splitting the data into subsets to create multiple variations of the same graph.

## The base layer

- The base layer of a `{ggplot2}` graph is created with the `ggplot()`{.R} function.
- We need to specify **two arguments**:
  - `data`: the dataset
  - `mapping`: a set of aesthetic mappings between variables in the data and visual properties
- Then, we need to provide at least <span class="hl-blue">one layer which describes how to render each observation</span> (usually created with a `geom` function).

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="70%"}
```r
ggplot(
  data = txhousing, 
  mapping = aes(x = volume, y = sales)
) +
  geom_point()
```
:::
::: {.column width="30%"}
- Each layer is added using the `+`{.R} operator.
:::
::::

## Our first graph with `{ggplot2}`


```{r}
p_txhousing <- ggplot(
  data = txhousing,
  mapping = aes(x = volume, y = sales)
) +
  geom_point()

p_txhousing
```

<!-- ![](figs/seance_3/txhousing.pdf) -->

# Aesthetics {.part}

## Geom layers and overriding aesthetics (1/2)

- The layers inherit aesthetics from `ggplot()`{.R}.
- If provided, new aesthetics will override those inherited from `ggplot()`{.R}.

```r
ggplot(
  data = txhousing, 
  mapping = aes(x = volume, y = sales)
) +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(colour = listings))
```

- `colour = listings`{.R} causes the colour of objects to vary with values of the variable `listings`.

## Geom layers and overriding aesthetics (2/2)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(
  data = txhousing, 
  mapping = aes(
    x = volume, 
    y = sales
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(colour = listings)
  )
```

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
<!-- ![](figs/seance_3/txhousing_colours.pdf) -->
```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(
  data = txhousing, 
  mapping = aes(
    x = volume, 
    y = sales
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(colour = listings)
  )
```

:::
::::

## Aesthetic attributes

- Multiple attributes are available, depending on the geom used, the most common are:
  - `x`, `y`: positioning along x-axis and y-axis, resp.,
  - `colour`: colour of objects,
  - `fill`: fill colour of objects (name or hexadecimal code),
  - `linetype`: how lines should be drawn (solid, dashed, dotted, …),
  - `shape`: shape of markers,
  - `size`: area of markers (for points), font size (for text),
  - `linesize`: thickness of the lines,
  - `alpha`: transparency (between 0 (transparent) and 1 (opaque)).

## Geoms and aesthetics

- Each geom has its required aesthetics.
  - E.g., `geom_point()`{.R} requires both `x` and `y`.
- Some aesthetics are not possible for some geoms.
  - E.g., while the `shape` aesthetic is used by `geom_point()`{.R}, it is not accepted by the `geom_bar()`{.R} function.
- Check the help pages or the online documentation, or even the [🎨 gallery](https://exts.ggplot2.tidyverse.org/gallery/).

# Usual visualizations {.part}

## Histogram

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(
  data = txhousing,
  mapping = aes(x = median)
) +
  geom_histogram(colour = "white")
```

A continuous variable (here: `median`) is cut into bins (default to 30). The number of observations (count) in each bin is reported.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the median housing sales in Texas between 2000 and 2015"
ggplot(
  data = txhousing,
  mapping = aes(x = median)
) +
  geom_histogram(colour = "white")
```

:::
::::

## Density plot

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(
  data = txhousing,
  mapping = aes(x = median)
) +
  geom_density(colour = "blue")
```

This type of representation can be viewed as a smoothed version of histograms.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Density of the median housing sales in Texas between 2000 and 2015 (kernel estimation)"
ggplot(
  data = txhousing,
  mapping = aes(x = median)
) +
  geom_density(colour = "blue")
```


:::
::::

## Bar plot

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(
  data = diamonds,
  mapping = aes(y = cut)
) +
  geom_bar(
    colour = "blue", fill = "grey"
  )
```

The width of the bar plot reflects the counts of each y-value.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Number of observation per quality of the cut in the `diamonds` dataset."
ggplot(
  data = diamonds,
  mapping = aes(y = cut)
) +
  geom_bar(
    colour = "blue", fill = "grey"
  )
```


:::
::::

## Scatter plot

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(
  data = txhousing,
  mapping = aes(
    x = volume, y = sales, 
    colour = listings,
    alpha = median,
    size = inventory
    )
) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Useful to represent covariation between two continuous variables.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Number of housing sales vs. total values of sales in Texas"
ggplot(
  data = txhousing,
  mapping = aes(
    x = volume, y = sales, 
    colour = listings,
    alpha = median,
    size = inventory
    )
) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```


:::
::::

## Line plot

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(
  data = txhousing,
  mapping = aes(
    x = date, y = sales, 
    group = city
    )
) +
  geom_line(
    colour = "blue", alpha = .3
  )
```

Useful to represent covariation between a continuous variable (y-axis) and an ordered variable (x-axis).
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Evolution of the number of housing sales in Texas. Each line represents a city."
ggplot(
  data = txhousing,
  mapping = aes(
    x = date, y = sales, 
    group = city
    )
) +
  geom_line(
    colour = "blue", alpha = .3
  )
```

:::
::::

# Labels {.part}

## Labels

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
The `labs()`{.R} function allows to change axis, legend, and plot labels.

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(
  data = txhousing, 
  mapping = aes(
    x = volume, y = sales,
    colour = listings
  )) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "No. housing sales vs. tot. volume",
    subtitle = "Texas, 2000 – 2015",
    x = "Total value of sales",
    y = "Number of sales",
    colour = "Total active listings"
  )
```

:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Number of housing sales vs. total values of sales in Texas."
ggplot(
  data = txhousing, 
  mapping = aes(
    x = volume, y = sales,
    colour = listings
  )) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "No. housing sales vs. tot. volume",
    subtitle = "Texas, 2000 – 2015",
    x = "Total value of sales",
    y = "Number of sales",
    colour = "Total active listings"
  )
```


:::
::::

# Exporting Graphs {.part}

## The `ggsave()`{.R} function

- The `ggsave()`{.R} function saves the last displayed plot (or a specific ggplot object if provided as argument).
- It supports many formats: **PNG** (good for presentations and web), **PDF** (for print and publications, i.e., your reports), JPEG, TIFF, SVG, EPS.
- Unless specified, in RStudio, the plot size and resolution of the 'Plots' tab is used (in inches).

```r
# Assuming p contains a ggplot2 graph:
ggsave(file = "figs/plot.pdf", p, width = 5, height = 3)
```

## Output quality

- When exporting a scatterplot, if the number of points is large, producing a PDF might not be a good idea: the file will be huge.
- To export a plot in PNG with a good resolution, the number of dots per inch (DPI) can be specified.

```r
# Assuming p contains a ggplot2 graph:
ggsave(
   file = "figs/plot.pdf", p, width = 5, height = 3,
   dpi = 300
)
```

## Scales

- Every aesthetic (colour, size, shape, x/y position, etc.) has a corresponding <span class="hl-blue">scale function</span>.
- Default scales are chosen automatically, but can be customized with a `scale_*` function.
- The type of scale depends on the data type of the variable:
  - **Continuous variables**: gradients, continuous axes, size scales,
  - **Discrete variables**: categorical palettes, shapes, breaks.

## Scales with a numeric variable

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(
  data = txhousing,
  mapping = aes(
    x = volume, y = sales
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(colour = listings)
  ) +
  scale_colour_gradient(
    "Total active listings",
    low = "yellow", high = "red"
  )
```

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The `listing` variable is numeric."
ggplot(
  data = txhousing,
  mapping = aes(
    x = volume, y = sales
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(colour = listings)
  ) +
  scale_colour_gradient(
    "Total active listings",
    low = "yellow", high = "red"
  )
```


:::
::::

## Scales with a discrete variable

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(
  data = sample_n(diamonds, size = 1000),
  mapping = aes(
    x = carat, y = price, colour = cut
  )
) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_manual(
    "Cut",
    values = c(
      "Fair" = "black", 
      "Good" = "blue", 
      "Very Good" = "darkgreen", 
      "Premium" = "palegreen", 
      "Ideal" = "yellow"
    )
  )
```

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The `cut` variable is discrete."
ggplot(
  data = sample_n(diamonds, size = 1000),
  mapping = aes(
    x = carat, y = price, colour = cut
  )
) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_manual(
    "Cut",
    values = c(
      "Fair" = "black", 
      "Good" = "blue", 
      "Very Good" = "darkgreen", 
      "Premium" = "palegreen", 
      "Ideal" = "yellow"
    )
  )
```

:::
::::

# Facetting {.part}

## Facetting

- Facetting corresponds to creating small subplots for subsets of data.
- Each panel shows the same plot for a different level of a variable.
- It makes it easier to compare patterns across groups.
- There are two main functions:
  - `facet_wrap()`{.R}: 1D wrapping of panels,
  - `facet_grid()`{.R}: 2D grid of panels.

## Facetting with `facet_wrap()`{.R}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(
  data = sample_n(diamonds, size = 5000),
  mapping = aes(
    x = carat, y = price
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = .5, alpha = .1) +
  facet_wrap(~ cut)
```

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Diamonds prices vs. their weights depending on the quality of the cut."
ggplot(
  data = sample_n(diamonds, size = 5000),
  mapping = aes(
    x = carat, y = price
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = .5, alpha = .1) +
  facet_wrap(~ cut)
```

:::
::::

## Facetting with `facet_grid()`{.R}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(
  data = sample_n(
    diamonds, 
    size = 5000
  ),
  mapping = aes(
    x = carat, y = price
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = .5, alpha = .1) +
  facet_grid(clarity ~ cut)
```

:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Diamonds prices vs. their weights depending on the quality of the cut and the clarity of the diamond."
ggplot(
  data = sample_n(
    diamonds, 
    size = 5000
  ),
  mapping = aes(
    x = carat, y = price
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = .5, alpha = .1) +
  facet_grid(clarity ~ cut)
```

:::
::::

## Codes for the graph showing the number of deaths in France (1/3) {#sec-appendix-codes-graph}

```r
# Source: https://www.insee.fr/en/statistiques/serie/000436394
file <- "data/deces_france_insee/monthly_values.csv"
deces <- read_csv2(
    file, skip = 4, 
    col_names = c("period", "deaths", "codes")
)

deces <- 
  deces |> 
  mutate(
    date = ym(period),
    month = month(date, label = TRUE),
    year = year(date)
  )
```

## Codes for the graph showing the number of deaths in France (2/3)

```r
# Prepare data for the plot: highlight 2003 and 2021
data_plot_deaths <- deces |> 
  mutate(
    year_excess = case_when(
      year == 2003 ~ "2003 (Drought)",
      year == 2020 ~ "2020 (Covid-19)",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    year_excess = factor(
      year_excess, 
      levels = c("2003 (Drought)", "2020 (Covid-19)", "Other")
    )
  )
```

## Codes for the graph showing the number of deaths in France (3/3)

```r
p_deaths <- ggplot(
  data = data_plot_deaths,
  mapping = aes(x = month, y = deaths, group = year, colour = year_excess)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = .8) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    NULL, values = c(
      "2003 (Drought)" = "blue",  "2020 (Covid-19)" = "red",

  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_number(suffix = "", scale = 1, big.mark = ",")
```
